message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
The document is still in my context, so "without looking back" doesn't apply to me the way it would to a person. I can't verify that I'm not drawing on it, and you should weigh my recall accordingly. Section 3's advice applies: check this against the text before relying on it.

## Title and opening

- The title is "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is about working with the team's material and with the people around you.
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because ordinary good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes. Each has earned a weight from its evidence, and your job is to hold it at exactly that weight.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three questions: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong?
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A plausible mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing. Note it, and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries the weight of its evidence and no more. Confidence is information about the speaker, not the world.
- Both errors are costly, but they are not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder.
- A caveat added to a sound result looks careful but is a misreport. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. Three months of the supplier's own figures should be weighed accordingly. A year of your own incoming inspection shouldn't be buried under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- This applies to papers, messages and reviews. Take all of it in and show that you have, by restating the substance briefly in your own terms.
- Restating isn't politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that answers three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it yet, and the next move is a question, not an answer.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is what your understanding makes available: an implication, a gap, the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply restates all five in a line each, answers four, and says plainly that the budget needs figures you don't yet have and when you will have them.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, your own notes and your memory are all compressions. Compression loses exactly the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific, check it against the primary material, however good the summary or confident the recollection.
- This applies most strongly to things you think you already know. The claims most likely to have drifted are the ones you've repeated to yourself many times.
- The source is the referee, not agreement among colleagues. A team that checks claims against each other instead of the data can drift into a shared mistake no one inside it can see.
- **Example:** a report remembered as "costs fell 12%" actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed

- Mark honestly which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open, and keep them that way.
- Closing early feels like progress, because a conclusion can be reported and a task ticked off. But it converts uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open, because closing it is uncomfortable or one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. Close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduces errors at two sites, but whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not "promising" and "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague gives is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point, a reading that didn't pass through your assumptions.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know will mostly return what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- So give reviewers the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find.
- Telling a fresh reader what you think doesn't just bias them. It removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse, when you are the fresh reader: read first, form your view, then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections when you have them. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it visibly, so others can check it and reverse it if needed.
- Share the draft before it feels finished. Make the call and show your reasoning. Push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context. It also stalls the work on your guess about what they'd say.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing you didn't already have. Only a real move gets a real reply, and the real reply is where you learn what you hadn't anticipated.
- This is not licence to act without regard for others. Moves that are hard to reverse or that commit other people's time deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- **Example:** rather than asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair:
  - **Inflating / deflating a claim.**
  - **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous, or dismissing one that is there to keep things moving.
  - **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
  - **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one:** dropping an idea at the first difficulty, or persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
  - **Deferring / dismissing:** accepting a claim because of who made it, or rejecting it for the same reason.
  - **Offloading / overriding:** asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what genuinely needs others' input.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.
